pros: Provides shortest paths to all nodes from a single source
Guaranteed to find correct shortest paths (provably correct)
Greedy approach makes it efficient for sparse graphs
Widely used and well-tested in production systems
Easy to reconstruct actual paths, not just distances
Can be optimized with different priority queue implementations
Easily modified for bidirectional search optimization
Forms the foundation for A* algorithm and other pathfinding variants
cons: Cannot handle negative edge weights (causes incorrect results)
Must examine all nodes to find shortest path to a single target
O(V²) time complexity for dense graphs without priority queue
Memory overhead for storing distances and predecessors
Priority queue operations add constant factor overhead
Single-source only; inefficient for all-pairs shortest paths
Struggles with graphs that have many equal-weight paths
Does not account for real-time traffic or dynamic edge weights
Inefficient for very large graphs unless combined with preprocessing
Requires graph to fit in memory (not naturally external-memory friendly)
